data.title: Labelbox Raises Over $100M to Expand AI Training and Enterprise Agents
data.ai_summary: Labelbox raised over $100 million in Series E financing led by Infinitum Partners. The company will use the funds to expand its reinforcement learning infrastructure and enterprise AI agent business, serving over 400 customers including most leading U.S. AI labs.
data.author: Win Warfield
data.full_text:
San Francisco-based Labelbox has raised more than $100 million in Series E financing led by Infinitum Partners, with participation from Wipro Ventures, Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), B Capital, Tau Ventures, Snowpoint Ventures, and other investors. The company seeks to expand its reinforcement learning infrastructure and enterprise AI agent business, as developers seek ways to improve models beyond their initial training.
Labelbox has developed two principal products. One called Horizon provides reinforcement learning environments and evaluation infrastructure for AI labs, letting models practice multistep tasks, receive feedback, and improve performance. The second, Recursion Managed Agents, targets enterprise customers. The company’s platform allows businesses to deploy groups of AI agents within existing applications, initiating tasks in response to schedules, alerts, and tickets.
“Every company will soon run on AI systems that learn from their own work. Getting there takes innovation at every layer, from sandbox infrastructure and the agent harness to reinforcement learning post-training. Labelbox brings those layers together in one platform, and this funding lets us push each one further, so that frontier labs and enterprises can build AI that gets better with every run,” said Manu Sharma, co-founder and CEO of Labelbox.
Sharma’s career has spanned aerospace engineering, robotics and software platforms. Before co-founding Labelbox, Sharma worked as a product manager at Planet Labs from 2017 to 2018, helping develop software for analyzing satellite imagery. As an early engineer at DroneDeploy, from 2014 to 2017, he worked on drone flight-control systems and the company’s application marketplace.
Earlier, Sharma co-founded Ardulab, also known as Infinity Aerospace, at NASA Ames Research Park. The venture developed open-source laboratory platforms for conducting scientific experiments aboard the International Space Station.
Labelbox said it serves more than 400 customers, including over 90% of leading U.S. AI labs. The company also uses more than 50 agents internally across engineering, research, product, sales, marketing and finance. It opened Recursion Managed Agents to enterprise customers earlier in October, extending a platform it previously used internally.
As AI developers seek to improve model reliability and close the gap between benchmark performance and real-world execution, Labelbox’s strategy combines training infrastructure with managed agents, potentially linking model development to enterprise deployment.

Deterministic verifiers score correctness consistently, while expert preference signals teach “taste” when multiple trajectories succeed. The platform operates at the scale of thousands of worlds and millions of graded trajectories, covering coding, computer use, research, multimodal, and voice domains, tuned to labs’ pass@k targets. Recursion Managed Agents: Enterprise Agents That Improve Themselves Recursion Managed Agents receive a goal, a trigger (schedule, alert, Slack message, webhook, or API call), and a rubric defining quality. A separate grader scores every run against the rubric and supplies evidence; agents revise when they fall short. Agents operate in multi agent (coordinator + specialists), team (parallel copies on a shared board), or auto modes. They connect to more than 100 business applications and any MCP server, with tools scoped by permission level and credentials held in a vault. Sessions run in isolated sandboxes with zero data retention at LLM providers. Compliance includes SOC 2 Type II, GDPR, CCPA, NIST 800-171, and PCI DSS. Pricing is per agent session hour. Internally, Labelbox runs 51 agents across 11 teams. In one documented example, a pull request review agent reduced median cost 32% across successive graded reviews while maintaining quality, with memory updated multiple times. Memory is curated automatically (once five new session reports exist, and at most once per hour) and remains reviewable and editable by customers. Both Horizon and Recursion rest on the same underlying principle: systems that improve from their own work through reflection on prior sessions, curated memory, and the ability to fine tune on their best outputs. data.full_text:
Labelbox, an AI platform supporting reinforcement learning for frontier models and managed agents for enterprises, has announced more than US$100 million in Series E financing. The round includes both equity and a credit facility and was led by Infinitum Partners, with participation from Wipro Ventures, Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), B Capital, Tau Ventures, Snowpoint Ventures, and others. The company disclosed the funding alongside news that it reached profitability in 2026 while growing more than fivefold year over year.
Funding and Growth
Labelbox works with more than 400 customers, including over 90% of leading U.S. AI labs, hyperscalers, startups, and Fortune 500 companies. The Series E financing will support continued research and engineering across Horizon and Recursion Managed Agents, as well as expansion of the teams bringing these products to customers. The company also plans to deepen its work with leading AI labs and hyperscalers on post-training programs.
Platform Approach
As AI models become capable of performing increasingly complex tasks, the next challenge is enabling them to learn from experience and reliably execute work in real-world environments. Labelbox is addressing this opportunity through two core products, Horizon and Recursion Managed Agents. Horizon focuses on reinforcement learning and evaluation for frontier labs, while Recursion Managed Agents supports enterprise fleets of agents that improve with every run.
Horizon for Frontier Labs
Horizon provides reinforcement learning environments, expert feedback, and evaluation infrastructure that help AI labs train and improve frontier models. Its environments simulate complex, multi-step work across coding, research, and other demanding tasks, enabling models to practice, receive feedback on their performance, and improve through reinforcement learning. Labelbox works with leading AI labs and hyperscalers on post-training programs that rely on these structured practice environments.
Recursion Managed Agents
Recursion Managed Agents enables companies to deploy fleets of AI agents inside the applications their teams already use. Agents can initiate work in response to schedules, alerts, tickets, and other triggers, coordinate across tools, and have their output evaluated against defined standards. Each completed run can inform the agent's memory, helping it improve how it approaches future tasks without manual retraining.
Leadership Perspective
"Every company will soon run on AI systems that learn from their own work," said Manu Sharma, CEO and co-founder of Labelbox. He noted that getting there takes innovation at every layer, from sandbox infrastructure and the agent harness to reinforcement learning post-training. Sharma added that Labelbox brings those layers together in one platform, and this funding lets the company push each one further so that frontier labs and enterprises can build AI that gets better with every run.
Enterprise Adoption
Labelbox already uses more than 50 agents internally across functions including engineering, research, product, sales, marketing, and finance. Earlier this month, the company opened Recursion Managed Agents to enterprise customers, extending its approach to continuous improvement beyond AI research labs. The platform lets enterprises deploy fleets of agents that coordinate across tools, respond to triggers such as schedules and tickets, and improve with every run.
With this Series E funding, Labelbox aims to help both frontier labs and enterprises build AI systems that learn from their own work and improve over time. The company combines agent infrastructure, sandbox environments, and reinforcement learning post-training systems to support the development and deployment of AI systems across demanding real-world tasks. Its profitability, fivefold year-over-year growth, and expanding customer base signal rising demand for AI platforms that enable continuous learning and reliable execution.

The activity reflects investor focus on AI infrastructure and specialized technologies.

More than $1.51 billion in newly announced funding transactions flowed into 10 major startups over the past 24 hours, alongside a separate €50 million investment in France. The biggest deals reveal a venture market financing two very different priorities: the infrastructure needed to run artificial intelligence at scale and specialized technologies that can solve expensive problems in healthcare, manufacturing, energy, and enterprise operations. San Francisco-based Modal led the day’s funding activity with a $750 million Series D at a $15.75 billion valuation, after reporting that its annualized revenue run rate surpassed $1 billion. Oxford biotech startup OMass Therapeutics secured $310 million to advance experimental treatments for hormonal and autoimmune diseases. Meanwhile, European energy-storage company Skeleton Technologies raised more than $100 million in Siemens-led financing, becoming a unicorn as it expands into the U.S. AI data center market. The activity extends across several layers of the AI economy. Salience Labs raised $125 million to commercialize optical networking chips that connect increasingly large GPU clusters. Labelbox announced more than $100 million in financing for reinforcement learning and enterprise AI agents. Harmonic Security secured $50 million to address the security risks created by employee AI use, while Duvo raised $32 million to automate operational processes across retailers and consumer-goods companies. Beyond AI software, India’s Scimplify raised $25 million to expand specialty-chemical and critical-materials production, with Hitachi Ventures leading the investment. France’s Dougs secured €50 million to accelerate AI-based accounting services. Boston-based Tamr raised $21 million to improve the fragmented enterprise data that increasingly autonomous AI systems depend on. The broader signal is that investors are financing the systems that make AI commercially useful, not just the models themselves. That includes computing capacity, optical networking, energy management, reliable data, security controls, and industry-specific execution. The 10 selected transactions represent more than $1.513 billion in disclosed dollar-denominated financing, plus €50 million. This is a headline transaction total, not a pure equity total: Labelbox’s financing includes a credit facility, while Skeleton’s transaction has not been fully broken down between primary investment and possible secondary share purchases. Those distinctions matter when measuring how much new capital actually enters startup balance sheets. The Macro Environment: AI Infrastructure Spending Meets a Growing Demand for Financial Discipline The latest funding activity arrives as venture investors confront an increasingly complicated AI economy. Demand for AI computing continues to grow, but the financial requirements of building and operating that infrastructure are becoming harder to ignore. GPU clusters require enormous capital commitments, substantial electricity supplies, specialized networking, and increasingly sophisticated workload-management systems. That creates opportunities for companies such as Modal, Salience Labs, and Skeleton Technologies. Each addresses a different constraint in the same market: Modal provides computing infrastructure developers can access without managing their own GPU clusters; Salience is developing optical switches to improve communication between processors; and Skeleton is building energy-storage systems designed to manage sudden fluctuations in data-center electricity demand. The distinction matters because AI infrastructure economics extend far beyond GPU prices. A data center can own expensive accelerators and still operate inefficiently because of networking bottlenecks, power fluctuations, poor utilization, or software overhead. Growing evidence also suggests public-market investors are becoming more sensitive to those costs. Shares of AI cloud provider CoreWeave fell sharply on October 14 amid concerns about borrowing costs and the sustainability of debt-financed infrastructure expansion. Financial Times reporting has also highlighted a slowdown in AI-related debt issuance as lenders become more selective. That does not mean private investors are abandoning AI infrastructure. Modal’s $750 million financing shows strong, ongoing demand for businesses that can turn compute into commercial revenue. But it suggests investors may increasingly distinguish between companies with demonstrated customer demand and infrastructure projects whose financial returns depend on uncertain future utilization. Outside computing infrastructure, OMass Therapeutics and Scimplify show that substantial capital remains available for difficult scientific and industrial problems. OMass is financing clinical development, where success ultimately depends on generating convincing evidence that experimental medicines work safely in patients. Scimplify is building a distributed manufacturing network for chemicals and critical materials, where customer qualification and production consistency determine commercial value. Those risks differ significantly from software economics. Yet both investments reflect a willingness to fund businesses whose capabilities require years of research, specialized facilities, regulatory expertise, and operating experience. The day’s enterprise software rounds introduce another important theme: AI is moving from experimentation into operational responsibility. Labelbox, Harmonic Security, Duvo, Tamr, and Dougs address different consequences of that transition, from reinforcement learning and agent execution to data accuracy, security, and regulated professional services. Together, the announcements suggest investors are looking beyond whether AI can perform a task. They increasingly want to know whether companies can deploy it reliably, measure its performance, control its risks, and generate durable revenue. Modal raises $750M in funding to expand AI infrastructure as annualized revenue run rate tops $1B San Francisco-based Modal raised $750 million in Series D financing at a $15.75 billion post-money valuation, led by Accel. Kleiner Perkins joined the investor base, while existing investors Menlo Ventures, General Catalyst, Redpoint, Lux Capital, Amplify Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures participated. The financing follows a $355 million Series C announced five months earlier. Modal disclosed the latest round on October 14 alongside a major operating milestone: the company says its annualized revenue run rate has surpassed $1 billion, with usage tripling since May and year-over-year growth exceeding 15x. Founded by Erik Bernhardsson, Modal provides cloud infrastructure designed around workloads that increasingly define AI development and deployment. Its platform supports model inference, training, reinforcement learning, and isolated computing environments in which AI agents can execute code. Instead of requiring developers to manage GPU servers, container infrastructure, scheduling systems, and networking, Modal provides software interfaces that let developers allocate computing resources as needed. The company says its infrastructure spans more than 20 cloud providers. Customers include DoorDash, Cognition, Ramp, Linear, Hebbia, Runway, and companies developing robotics and drug-discovery applications. A billion-dollar run rate changes the investment case Modal’s financial milestone is important, but the terminology deserves attention. Annualized revenue run rate is not the same as annual recurring revenue. A run rate extrapolates current revenue activity into an annual figure. It does not necessarily represent contractual commitments that customers will maintain for the next 12 months. That distinction matters most for usage-based infrastructure businesses, where customer spending can fluctuate with workloads and demand. Modal also reports that its Sandboxes product, which provides isolated environments for executing code, has reached a $300 million annualized run rate. The product has become especially relevant as coding agents generate and execute more software. For investors, Modal represents a bet that the next major software infrastructure category will be built around AI workloads rather than traditional application hosting. Its competitive position depends on developer experience, workload efficiency, reliability, pricing, and the ability to manage computing capacity across different providers. However, the company faces substantial competition from established cloud platforms and specialized AI infrastructure providers. The biggest question is whether its software architecture can maintain attractive margins as customers demand lower inference costs and greater computing capacity. Funding Details Startup: Modal

Valuation: $15.75 billion post-money OMass Therapeutics raises $310M in funding to advance treatments for hormonal and autoimmune diseases Oxford-based OMass Therapeutics raised $310 million (£230 million) in an oversubscribed Series C financing, co-led by Bain Capital Life Sciences, Forbion, and Novo Holdings. Additional investors include Janus Henderson Investors, SV Health Investors, and Jefferson Life Sciences. Existing shareholders Syncona, Oxford Science Enterprises, GV, Northpond Ventures, Sanofi Ventures, British Business Bank, and the University of Oxford also participated. OMass is a biotechnology company developing small-molecule medicines for diseases involving difficult biological targets. The company originated from research conducted in Professor Dame Carol Robinson’s laboratory at the University of Oxford. Its drug-discovery platform combines native mass spectrometry, specialized biochemistry, and chemistry techniques to study proteins and their interactions in biologically relevant environments. The goal is to identify medicines that can act on targets that have historically been difficult to address. Investors are financing clinical evidence, not simply scientific discovery The largest portion of OMass’s new financing will support development of OMS1620, an experimental medicine targeting the melanocortin-2 receptor. The company is developing the drug for congenital adrenal hyperplasia and ACTH-dependent Cushing’s syndrome, conditions involving abnormal hormone regulation. OMass plans to advance the medicine through Phase 2 clinical development. It will also use the financing to support an experimental SLC15A4 inhibitor intended for lupus and other diseases associated with abnormal immune signaling. The investment is significant because OMass is moving toward clinical milestones that could establish whether its scientific approach produces meaningful therapeutic benefits. That creates a different risk profile from AI software. A promising discovery platform can identify potential medicines, but clinical trials must establish safety and efficacy in patients. Even substantial financing cannot eliminate that uncertainty. The participation of Bain Capital Life Sciences, Forbion, Novo Holdings, and established biotechnology investors indicates confidence in the company’s pipeline and research approach. Still, the next material valuation events will likely depend on clinical data rather than funding announcements. For founders, OMass illustrates the importance of financing long-duration scientific programs around specific technical milestones. For investors, it represents a bet that differentiated biology can support valuable medicines even in a market where clinical development remains expensive and uncertain. Valuation: Not disclosed Salience Labs raises $125M in funding to scale optical networking chips for AI data centers Oxford-based Salience Labs raised $125 million in Series B financing led by Bullhound Capital. AMD Ventures, Intel Capital, SBI Group, Hudson River Trading, and British Business Bank joined the round. Existing shareholders Applied Ventures, Oxford Science Enterprises, Cambridge Innovation Capital, and Silicon Catalyst Ventures also participated. Salience develops photonic chips designed to improve communication inside AI data centers. The technology addresses a problem that becomes more significant as computing clusters grow. Thousands of GPUs may need to communicate across multiple racks while training or running increasingly complex AI models. Traditional electrical networking systems can introduce limitations involving bandwidth, latency, energy consumption, and the cost of moving data. Salience is developing optical circuit switches that use light to connect computing resources. Its architecture is designed to improve connectivity while reducing overhead associated with conventional switching infrastructure. AI computing is becoming a networking problem Salience recently demonstrated a 64-port optical circuit switch at ECOC 2026. The company plans to develop larger 128-port and 256-port products while expanding manufacturing capabilities. Its technology draws on more than a decade of research associated with the University of Oxford and the University of Münster. The investment’s strategic significance is reinforced by AMD Ventures and Intel Capital’s participation. Both investors operate in industries directly affected by the growing complexity of AI computing infrastructure. For investors, Salience offers exposure to AI growth without requiring the company to compete in the GPU market itself. As computing clusters grow, the network connecting processors can influence overall system performance and cost. However, optical networking technologies must meet demanding commercial requirements. Salience will need to demonstrate manufacturing yields, reliability, integration with existing infrastructure, and measurable economic advantages. The company also faces competition from established networking vendors and other photonics startups. Its ability to move from a successful demonstration into high-volume production will determine whether the technology becomes a commercially significant part of AI infrastructure. The transaction includes a broader strategic relationship involving Siemens’s investment and rights to commercialize Skeleton technology. A separate shareholder disclosure also identified a partial secondary stake sale to Siemens, meaning the precise amount of fresh primary capital cannot be determined from the public announcements. Skeleton develops energy-storage systems based on supercapacitors and its proprietary Curved Graphene material. Unlike conventional batteries, which are designed primarily to store large amounts of energy for extended periods, supercapacitors can respond extremely quickly to changing power demands. That capability is becoming relevant to AI data centers. GPU clusters can shift between operating states in milliseconds, creating abrupt changes in electricity consumption. Those fluctuations can stress electrical infrastructure and complicate efficient operation of large computing systems. Skeleton’s products are designed to manage rapid power changes close to computing workloads. Siemens is buying access to a data center infrastructure category Skeleton says its technology can deliver energy savings of up to 40% in certain applications and improve GPU performance by double-digit percentages. Those are company-reported performance claims, not independently established results across all AI data centers. The Siemens partnership matters because it offers a potential route into major industrial and hyperscale infrastructure projects. Siemens plans to integrate Skeleton’s products into its broader electrical infrastructure offering, and the companies are collaborating on AI data center technologies. Skeleton intends to invest more than $200 million in manufacturing expansion and research activities in Silicon Valley. That figure represents planned expenditure, not the amount Siemens is newly investing. The company is also planning U.S. manufacturing capacity that would support production from energy-storage cells through complete systems. For investors, Skeleton represents a way to participate in AI infrastructure growth through electricity management. Its competitive advantage may depend more on material science, manufacturing capability, system integration, and customer relationships than on software alone. Remaining questions include commercial margins, manufacturing expansion costs, customer concentration, and whether performance improvements translate into attractive economics for data center operators. Labelbox said on October 14, 2026, that it raised more than $100 million in Series E financing at a $1.25 billion pre-money valuation, in a round led by Infinitum Partners that combines equity with a credit facility. Wipro Ventures, Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), B Capital, Tau Ventures, and Snowpoint Ventures also participated, among others. Chief executive and co-founder Manu Sharma detailed the terms in a company blog post, and the company said the financing will support continued research and engineering across its two core products, Horizon and Recursion Managed Agents, as well as expansion of the teams bringing those products to customers. Sharma wrote that access to compute will be central to the company’s next chapter, noting that Infinitum’s John Yetimoglu was an early investor in Groq and is now involved in building large-scale compute infrastructure at GroqCloud. Company Position and History Labelbox stated that it reached profitability in 2026 while growing more than fivefold year over year. The company reports more than 400 customers, including over 90% of leading U.S. AI labs, and says its base spans frontier AI labs, hyperscalers, startups, and Fortune 500 companies. Sharma, Brian, and Dan founded Labelbox in 2018. In a founder’s note, Sharma wrote that he came to the United States to learn to design and build aircraft and rockets, working on computational fluid dynamics and neural networks, and that his later roles at DroneDeploy and Planet Labs showed him how much of the opportunity in machine learning sat in data. The post describes the company’s history in three chapters: training-data software for people building AI; reinforcement-learning environments built after what Sharma calls the ChatGPT moment, when the most capable models began improving by practicing real work; and agents, which the company built for itself first before opening the system to customers. Sharma also wrote that Labelbox builds each layer of its platform itself: an agent harness designed for ultra-long-horizon agents, sandbox infrastructure that runs millions of virtual machines, its own reinforcement-learning post-training infrastructure, and an expert network of more than 4 million people. Horizon Reinforcement-Learning Environments According to the company, Horizon’s WorldSim system builds simulated companies, with code, dashboards, spreadsheets, decks, and documents filled with realistic business data, in which a model attempts a difficult multi-step task end to end while every step is recorded as a trajectory. Deterministic verifiers score each trajectory the same way on every run, and when two trajectories are both correct, an expert’s preference teaches the model what Sharma calls taste. The company describes operating at a scale of thousands of worlds and millions of graded trajectories, tuned to a lab’s pass@k targets across coding, computer use, research, multimodal, and voice work. The Horizon product page lists domains that include autonomous AI research, agent coding and software engineering, multimodal knowledge work, voice with agentic tool use, computer use, and cybersecurity. Sharma wrote that Labelbox now works with 90% of the leading frontier AI labs and hyperscalers. Recursion Managed Agents The funding announcement states that Labelbox opened Recursion Managed Agents to enterprise customers earlier in October 2026. Under the product’s design, a Managed Agent receives a goal, a trigger such as a schedule, an alert, a Slack message, a webhook, or an API call, and a rubric defining what good work looks like. A separate grader agent scores every run against the rubric line by line and points to evidence for each call; when the work misses, the agent revises it. Agents can operate in three modes: multi-agent, in which a coordinator chains specialists that each carry their own model, instructions, tools, and permissions; team, in which copies of an agent split work on a shared board and check each other’s results; and auto, the default, in which the agent decides for itself when a job needs specialists or a team. The company says agents work across more than 100 business applications and any MCP server, with every tool scoped as read only, changes data, or destructive and credentials held in a vault so the model never sees them. Sessions run in isolated sandboxes, and Labelbox says the platform runs with zero data retention at every LLM provider. Its listed compliance program covers SOC 2 Type II, GDPR, CCPA, NIST 800-171, and PCI DSS. Pricing is set per agent session hour, with compute and model spend combined in one estimate, and existing Labelbox enterprise customers receive a one-time $100 credit. Describing the company’s internal rollout in a product launch post dated October 8, 2026, Labelbox wrote, “The surprise wasn’t that agents could do the work. It was how quickly they got better at it.” The company reports running 51 agents across 11 teams, spanning software engineering, reliability, security, machine-learning research, evals, product, finance, sales, strategy, and procurement. In one internal example, Labelbox said its pull-request review agent ran 39 graded reviews on a single agent version and model, and that across the 33 reviews that passed the grader, the median cost fell from $13.15 for the first 11 reviews to $8.90 for the last 11, 32% less per review, while the agent’s memory was updated 15 times and time per review held at about 27 minutes. Under the product’s memory mechanics, once five new session reports exist, and at most once an hour, a curator agent reads them and updates the agent’s memory; customers can browse what an agent has learned and delete any lesson that no longer holds.
